segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mr Rowe had not forgiven Miss Vane for the business of the verse. It had happened in the library in January. He had been giving Mrs Hale the substance of Sunday's sermon, warmly, at some length, and had quoted his text with one word wrong. Miss Vane was at the shelf with her back to him. She said the right words without turning round, in the tone of a woman reading a shop bill, and went on with what she was doing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Two customers heard her. Mrs Hale repeated the whole of it for a fortnight, always kindly, which was worse. That Miss Vane had been right was not the point. Nobody had asked her, and a man who has been at his books since six may be allowed one word.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Miss Vane had her own account, and hers was of February. Old Nan Corbin at the mill cottages had been laid up with her hip, and Rowe went to her every Thursday and read her improving matter until she fell asleep out of self-defence. Judith wrote out a list of six novels the library had and gave it to him at the counter.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: I do not think circulating trash is what she wants.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Rowe, and gave it back across the counter.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: Have you read any of them?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He had not, and said so, and thought no more about it. She kept the list in the ledger drawer for eleven weeks before she burnt it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So matters stood on the Thursday when Mrs Pike came to the apothecary's back parlour, sat down without being asked twice, and got to her subject before her bonnet strings were undone.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: Now, my dear, you are the only practical creature in this parish. It is to be Wednesday, and it must be a dinner, for you cannot introduce anybody over tea. I shall have Miss Marchmont, and Mr Rowe, and your brother if he will leave off his powders. You will not mind the trouble. You never do mind trouble.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: You wish me to order your dinner for you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Judith.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: I wish you to save it. My Hannah cannot be trusted with a joint and a sauce in the same afternoon. And you shall see the young lady before anybody else in Amberlight, which is worth something.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Judith said she would. She told herself it was for want of anything else to do between Thursday and Wednesday. It was also because she wished to see what a Marchmont looked like, the family having held the living since her grandfather's time without once coming into it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What she had not counted on was Mr Rowe. Mrs Pike sent him to her twice on Friday and once on Monday, with questions she could have answered herself in half the time.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: Mrs Pike asks whether there are flowers to be had. She particularly said white.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Rowe, from the doorway, having got no further in.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: There is guelder rose in the lane past the smithy. It will be over by Wednesday, but it will be white until then.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: Thank you. That is very exact.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he said.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: You may tell her the ham is spoken for and the pigeons are not. She will want to know which before she asks me herself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Every sentence was correct and none of them was meant, and each went away certain that the other had been the more disagreeable of the two.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the Monday evening Owen Vane came through from the dispensary with his sleeves still turned up, and found his sister writing out a list of what Mrs Pike's larder wanted.

segments.speaker: Mr Owen Vane
segments.text: That is the third paper you have covered for that woman's table.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said Owen.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: It is a large table.

segments.speaker: Mr Owen Vane
segments.text: It is a small parish. You have been very taken up with the curate's dinner, Judith, for a woman who cannot abide the curate.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She looked at the paper, and then at the window, and did not find anything to say to him.
